title: REVES: REvision and VErification–Augmented Training for Test-Time Scaling

paper.title: REVES: REvision and VErification–Augmented Training for Test-Time Scaling
paper.abstract: Abstract Test-time scaling via sequential revision has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. However, standard post-training methods primarily optimize single-shot objectives, creating a fundamental misalignment with multi-step inference dynamics. While recent work treats this as multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL), conventional approaches optimize over the multi-step trajectories directly, failing to further exploit the high-quality mistakes in intermediate steps that model can learn from correcting them. We propose a two-stage iterative framework that alternates between online data/prompt augmentation and policy optimization. By converting the intermediate steps (“near-miss” answers) in the successful recovery trajectories into decoupled revision and verification prompts, our approach concentrates training on both effective answer transformation and error identification. This approach enables efficient off-policy data generation and reduces the computational overhead of long-horizon sampling compared to standard multi-turn RL. On LiveCodeBench, using publicly available test cases as feedback, we observe gains of +6.5 points over the RL baseline and +4.0 points over standard multi-turn training. Beyond coding, our approach matches the previously reported SOTA result on circle packing while using the smallest base model (4B) and far fewer rollouts than the much larger evolutionary search systems. Math results under ground-truth verification further confirm improved correction ability. It also generalizes to out-of-distribution constraint-satisfaction puzzles such as n_queens and mini_sudoku, where correctness is defined entirely by problem constraints. Code is available at https://github.com/yxliu02/REVES.git .

Code is available at https://github.com/yxliu02/REVES.git . 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) deployed in challenging settings rarely produce a correct answer on the first attempt; real-world workflows routinely loop back with feedback. A growing family of test-time scaling (TTS) algorithms formalizes this pattern, including sequential revision ( Madaan et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ) , tree search ( Inoue et al., 2025 ) , evolutionary refinement ( Lee et al., 2025b ) , and best-of- N N with a verifier ( Chow et al., 2025 ) . They all share a single primitive: given a problem, a previous attempt, and feedback, produce an improved response. This raises a basic question: can we design a post-training algorithm that explicitly improves a model’s test-time sequential revision capability? We focus on sequential revision (SR) because gains on SR transfer to the rest of the family: every revision-using TTS algorithm eventually calls the policy on revise-from-prior-attempt inputs. SR is also a strong TTS algorithm in its own right, matching or surpassing tree search and evolutionary refinement on planning tasks (Figure 2 ). Theorem 3.1 shows that increasing the policy’s one-step revision value on SR-induced inputs also raises J ϕ J_{\phi} for every revision-using TTS algorithm that covers SR’s revision inputs, up to small drift terms. How, then, do we post-train an LLM to optimize the SR objective J ϕ SR J_{{\phi_{\mathrm{SR}}}} ? Standard post-training, RLHF ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , RLVR, and GRPO ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ) , optimizes a single-shot expected reward, which is fundamentally misaligned with the multi-step nature of test-time deployment. The natural fix is multi-turn RL on revision rollouts, but trajectory-level credit broadcasts assign path-dependent credit. Take a wrong, wrong, correct rollout: every per-turn log-probability gradient receives the same positive credit, including the wrong intermediates. Per rollout this credit is biased, and only cancels in expectation across many rollouts. We propose REVES, a two-stage iterative framework that targets the SR objective J ϕ SR J_{{\phi_{\mathrm{SR}}}} directly through its per-state structure. We show that J ϕ SR J_{{\phi_{\mathrm{SR}}}} decomposes exactly into a weighted sum of per-state one-step recovery probabilities along visited rollouts (Lemma 4.1 ), exposing single-state, single-turn gradients with no horizon credit assignment. REVES is an offline realization of this per-state training signal: each epoch, it runs SR rollouts under the current policy, retains those that succeed within budget, converts the intermediate (“near-miss”) answers into decoupled revision and verification prompts, and trains with standard single-turn RL on the augmented prompt set; the next epoch refreshes the augmentation. This concentrates training on per-state recovery and avoids both the bias of trajectory broadcasts and the cost of long-horizon online sampling. Empirically, on LiveCodeBench with public test cases as feedback, REVES achieves + 6.5 +6.5 points over the single-shot RL baseline and + 4.0 +4.0 points over standard multi-turn training. On the circle packing benchmark, a Qwen3-4B base trained with REVES matches the previously reported best results from much larger evolutionary search systems built on Gemini-2.0 Pro/Flash and Qwen3-8B. Math benchmarks (MATH500, AIME24/25) show consistent improvements under both ground-truth and self-confidence stopping, and the trained policies generalize to out-of-distribution constraint-satisfaction puzzles (n_queens, mini_sudoku). Beyond standalone SR, REVES improves every revision-using TTS algorithm we tested (MCTS, AB-MCTS variants, Mind Evolution), in line with the conditional bound in Theorem 3.1 . Our contributions are threefold: 1. Conceptual. We formulate test-time scaling as a meta-RL problem and show that improving sequential revision also improves any revision-using TTS algorithm that covers SR’s revision inputs (Theorem 3.1 ). 2. Methodological. We exactly decompose J ϕ SR J_{{\phi_{\mathrm{SR}}}} into per-state one-step recovery probabilities (Lemma 4.1 ) and propose REVES, a two-stage framework that recasts intermediate near-miss answers as decoupled revision and verification prompts trained with single-turn RL, avoiding the path-dependent credit assignment of multi-turn RL. 3. Empirical. REVES delivers consistent test-time gains across math, coding, out-of-distribution puzzles, and circle packing, and improves every revision-using TTS algorithm we evaluated. 2 Related Work Test-time-aware post-training. A growing line of work shows the importance of aligning the post-training objective with the intended test-time inference strategy. For parallel-sampling families, this includes optimizing pass@ k k ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Walder & Karkhanis, 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) when deployment uses best-of- N N , majority voting ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , or learned verifiers ( Chow et al., 2025 ) . Our deployment is structurally different: the test-time strategies we care about, including sequential revision, MCTS variants, and Mind Evolution, are all revision-using algorithms whose calls take as input a previous attempt together with its feedback. Aligning training with this inference family therefore requires a different objective. Training sequential revision capability. Closer to our setting, several prior methods explicitly train the policy to revise, including supervised and preference-based approaches ( Qu et al., 2024 ; Xiong et al., 2025 ) , RL-based approaches ( Kumar et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025a ) , and multi-turn RL methods that incorporate per-turn natural-language or numerical critiques ( Jain et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Our work shares the broader goal of strengthening the model’s revision capability, but differs in framing: we primarily focus on how to align training with the test-time objective of a revision-using inference strategy. Weakness-driven data synthesis and guided exploration. SwS ( Liang et al., 2025 ) synthesizes new problems targeting the model’s weaknesses using strong external teacher models, and POPE ( Qu et al., 2026 ) uses privileged oracle hints to guide on-policy exploration on hard problems. These methods are orthogonal to ours: they target single-shot pass@1, whereas REVES targets a fundamentally different test-time objective. 3 Test-Time Scaling as a Meta-RL Problem Setup and two motivating examples. We fix notation used throughout the paper. Denote by 𝒳 \mathcal{X} the distribution over input problems, 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} the answer space, and r ⋆ : 𝒳 × 𝒴 → [ 0 , 1 ] r^{\star}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to[0,1] the ground-truth reward, where r ⋆ ​ ( x , y ) = 1 r^{\star}(x,y)=1 indicating a fully correct answer. We focus on the verifiable-reward regime where r ⋆ r^{\star} is computable during both training and at test time, e.g., public test-case execution for code, and constraint satisfaction for puzzles. When r ⋆ r^{\star} is unavailable at test time, a surrogate stopping rule replaces it (Section 4 ). We model the LLM as a policy π θ \pi_{\theta} in RL parameterized by θ \theta . At deployment, an LLM rarely operates by a single call to π θ \pi_{\theta} ; instead a test-time scaling (TTS) algorithm ϕ \phi orchestrates up to K K policy calls and extracts a final answer y ^ ∈ 𝒴 \hat{y}\in\mathcal{Y} .
